title: The Language
notes_he: שיעור 2.1 הוא תצוגה מקדימה. הוא נותן הגדרות ולא את שלבי השיטה.

slide: Three words we'll use in every lesson
narration: In this lesson we'll pin down three words we'll use in every lesson from now on: goal, task and constraint.
They sound simple. But most planning problems start when people mix them up.

slide: The end state. What has to be true when we're done.
Example: Everyone who eats is full.
narration: A goal is the end state. It describes what has to be true when we're done.
Not what we do. What is true at the end.
A simple test: can you picture the moment it's done? Everyone who eats is full. You can picture that.

slide: An action that moves you toward the goal.
narration: A task is an action. It usually starts with a verb: buy, cook, call, send.
A task is only worth doing if it moves you toward the goal.
And tasks can change. If the store is closed, buying groceries stops being a good task. But the goal is still there.

slide: A limit you have to work within.
Examples: Lunch is at one. We have twenty dollars. No peanuts.
narration: A constraint is a limit. Time, money, rules, things you can't use.
Lunch is at one o'clock. We have twenty dollars. One of the kids is allergic to peanuts.
Constraints don't tell you where to go. They tell you which roads are closed.

slide: A task treated as a goal: you keep doing it after it stops helping.
A constraint packed into the goal: when the limit moves, the goal seems to fail.
narration: Why does this matter?
When a task is treated as a goal, people keep doing it even after it stops helping.

When a constraint is packed into the goal, every change in the limit feels like failure. Lunch at one becomes lunch at a quarter past one, and suddenly the whole plan feels broken. Even though everyone still gets fed.

slide: Your manager says: Get the report to the client by Friday.
narration: Now let's try it at work. Your manager says: get the report to the client by Friday.
Which part is which? Send the report is a task. By Friday is a constraint.
So where's the goal? It isn't there. And that's very common.
The goal is what should be true after the client reads the report. Maybe the client approves the next phase. Maybe they have what they need to make a decision.

slide: When the goal is missing, ask:
What should be true when this is done?
narration: When the goal is missing, ask. One simple question works almost every time: what should be true when this is done?
Most managers are glad to answer it. And once you know the answer, you can do a much better job than just sending a file on time.

slide: Constraint: a limit you work within
narration: So, three words. A goal is the end state. A task is an action that moves you toward it. A constraint is a limit you work within.
In the next lesson, we'll look at one more word that causes a lot of confusion.
There's one word we'll avoid in this course, and it's worth a few minutes to explain why. The word is mission.

slide: “Your mission today” = a job to do
narration: In everyday business English, a mission sounds like a big purpose. A company's mission statement is about why it exists.
But in many workplaces, a mission is simply a job you were given to do. Your mission today is to finish the report.

slide: In military planning, a mission holds both:
narration: In military planning, a mission usually holds both: what to do, and why, in one sentence.
That works when everyone has been trained to read it that way.
In most offices, people hear only the first half, the task. And the purpose gets lost.
Mission isn't the only slippery word. Objective, target, deliverable, even priority.
Each one can mean a goal, a task or a constraint, depending on who's talking.
So in this course we'll stick to three plain words: goal, task and constraint.
When you hear them, you'll know exactly what they mean.

slide: When someone hands you a mission, ask:
1. What do you need me to do?
2. What should be true when it's done?
narration: And when someone at work hands you a mission, or an objective, or a deliverable, translate it.
Ask two questions. What do you need me to do? And what should be true when it's done?
The first answer is the task. The second is the goal.
Next, a short quiz to make sure the three words stick.

quiz.q: Which of these is a goal?
quiz.why: A goal is an end state. Calling back is a task, and replying within one day is a constraint.

quiz.q: “We have a budget of five thousand dollars.” This is a:
quiz.why: A budget is a limit you work within. It doesn't say where you're going.

quiz.q: “Prepare the slides for the meeting.” This is a:
quiz.why: It's an action that starts with a verb. The goal behind it is still unknown.

quiz.q: Your manager says: “Finish the onboarding guide by Thursday.” What is missing?
quiz.why: Finish the guide is the task, and by Thursday is the constraint. Nothing says what should be true when it's done.

quiz.q: Which question helps you find a missing goal?
options: What should be true when this is done?
Who else is working on this?
quiz.why: The other two questions are useful, but only this one asks about the end state.

quiz.q: “Every new hire can use the system on their first day.” This is a:
quiz.why: It describes what is true at the end. You can picture the moment it's done.

quiz.q: Why is it a problem to pack a constraint into the goal?
options: It makes the goal too long to remember.
When the limit changes, the goal seems to fail, even if it can still be reached.
Constraints should never be written down.
quiz.why: Keep limits separate. Then a change in a limit changes the plan, not the goal.

quiz.q: A team keeps running a weekly meeting that no longer helps anyone. What most likely happened?
options: They treated a task as if it were the goal.
quiz.why: The meeting was a task. Once it stopped serving the goal, it should have changed or stopped.
